description: A plain-English guide to Pidyon HaBen — the mitzvah, the five silver shekels, the 31st day, and the ceremony — for families redeeming a firstborn son.
text:
A Bullion Trading Tradition
פִּדְיוֹן הַבֵּן
Pidyon HaBen — The Redemption of the Firstborn Son
One of the most meaningful reasons we sell silver has nothing to do with investing. Several times each year we help families preparing for a Pidyon HaBen. For most, it is the first — and only — time they will ever buy silver coins, so the questions are many, and completely understandable.
Educational only — for your family’s situation, always follow your rabbi.
פִּדְיוֹן הַבֵּן
ה׳
PIDYON HABEN
Pidyon HaBen means, literally, “redemption of the son.” It is a positive mitzvah from the Torah (Exodus 13 and Numbers 18): the father of a qualifying firstborn son gives a
kohen
the value of five biblical shekels of silver, and in doing so redeems his son. It is done on the baby’s thirty-first day, and it is a joyful, once-in-a-lifetime occasion.
Why a redemption at all? After the Exodus, the firstborn of Israel were consecrated to serve in the sanctuary. That role later passed to the tribe of Levi — so a firstborn who is
not
of priestly or Levite lineage is symbolically “redeemed” from a kohen, in silver, the metal the Torah names for sacred valuations.
The price
5
silver shekels of the sanctuary (Num. 18:16)
The day
31st
after birth — day one counts from birth
In silver
≈100g
pure silver, commonly ≈3.2 troy oz
The five shekels are counted out in the Book of Numbers
In the wilderness census, the Levites were designated to take the place of the firstborn in sacred service — one Levite for one firstborn. But the firstborn outnumbered the Levites, and the surplus had to be redeemed in silver. That is where the number five is fixed.
22,273
Israelite firstborn counted
Numbers 3:43
−
22,000
Levites, one per firstborn
Numbers 3:39
=
273
surplus firstborn, with no Levite to replace them
Numbers 3:46
Each of the 273 was redeemed at
five shekels
of silver (Num. 3:47) — 1,365 shekels in all, given to Aaron and his sons (Num. 3:50–51). That one-time desert redemption becomes the permanent mitzvah of Numbers 18:15–16.
Why did the firstborn lose the role in the first place? The verse simply designates the Levites in their place. A widely-cited tradition —
the sages explain
— teaches that the firstborn forfeited the privilege through their part in the sin of the Golden Calf, while the tribe of Levi stayed loyal.
Is your son obligated?
Walk down the path. Any single answer that steps off it means there is no Pidyon HaBen. This is a guide to understanding, not a ruling — the edge cases are exactly the ones to bring to your rabbi.
Q1
Is he his mother’s firstborn?
Her first pregnancy to term — even if the father already has children from another mother.
If not
Exempt — the womb was opened before
Q2
Was he born naturally — not by cesarean?
A peter rechem “opens the womb.” A C-section birth does not qualify (nor does a naturally-born son after one).
If C-section
Exempt
Q3
Was there no prior qualifying pregnancy loss?
A loss past a certain stage can count as a first opening of the womb. Timing is decisive and often uncertain.
Depends
Consult a rabbi
Q4
Is the father not a Kohen or Levi?
A priestly or Levite father carries that sanctity already — no redemption is needed.
If he is
Exempt
Q5
Is the mother not the daughter of a Kohen or Levi?
A bat-Kohen or bat-Levi mother exempts her son even when the father is a plain Israelite.
If she is
Exempt
If the path held all the way down
Your firstborn son is obligated in Pidyon HaBen
on his 31st day — confirm the specifics with your rav

Ask a rabbi
Depends on the stage — handled gently, case by case
A quick reference — not a substitute for a rabbi’s ruling on your case.
How much silver — and why the opinions differ
The Torah fixes the price as five sanctuary shekels of silver. Rendering that in grams depends on the disputed weight of the ancient coin, so authorities land in a range. The good news for a family: a set built to the high end simply clears them all.
1
2
3
4
5
Five coins to mirror the
five shekalim
. Some families add a sixth as a safeguard, in case one runs light.
Pure silver required, by opinion
Grams of pure silver for the full five-shekel redemption.
Sephardic minimum
Rambam · Ḥacham Ovadia
≈ 90 g
Ashkenazi minimum
Rav Chaim Naeh
≈ 96 g
Common practice
the customary about 100 g
≈ 100 g
Coin-set buffer
clears every opinion
≈ 117 g
A note on the numbers.
The two classic authorities on halachic weights — Rav Chaim Naeh and the Chazon Ish — both land near
96–102 g
for the five shekels of Pidyon HaBen. The larger
≈117 g
seen on many dedicated coin sets is not a specific stringency; it is a deliberate buffer (five ≈26 g coins at 90% silver) chosen so a single set satisfies every opinion at once. Your family should follow your own rav’s or community’s custom.
The thirty-first day
The day of birth counts as day one. After thirty completed days, the redemption is held on the thirty-first — with one gentle exception.
Day 1
Birth
Counts as the first day
Day 30
30 completed days
The waiting period
Day 31
Pidyon HaBen
Ashkenazi: daytime of the 31st · Sephardi: evening before
Shabbat / Yom Tov
Deferred
to the next permitted weekday
Not deferred on Chol HaMoed, Chanukah or Purim — the ceremony is held on those days.
The ceremony
The heart of it is a short scripted exchange between the father and the kohen, two blessings, and a blessing over the child, set within a festive meal (a
seudat mitzvah
). The wording below is the representative Ashkenaz text; rites vary by community.
The child is presented
At a daytime seudat mitzvah, the baby — often dressed in finery on a silver tray — is brought before the kohen with the five silver coins. A minyan is preferred.
The father declares, and the kohen asks
The kohen
“Which would you rather have — your firstborn son, or the five coins you are obligated to give me for his redemption?”
The father
My Israelite wife has borne me this firstborn son.
The father chooses his son
The father
“I want my firstborn son — and here are the five coins required of me for his redemption.”
He then recites two blessings, just before handing over the silver:
בָּרוּךְ… עַל פִּדְיוֹן הַבֵּן
“…who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of a son.”
שֶׁהֶחֱיָנוּ
“…who has granted us life, sustained us, and enabled us to reach this occasion.” (Sheheḥeyanu)
The coins are handed over, and the kohen blesses the child
The father gives the five coins to the kohen. Holding them over the child, the kohen declares a formula of substitution — “may this child enter into life, Torah, and the fear of Heaven” — then places his hand on the baby’s head and gives the Priestly Blessing, opening with “May G‑d make you like Ephraim and Menasheh.”
Wine, and the festive meal
The kohen recites the blessing over a cup of wine, and the celebration continues. In many communities it is customary to hand out cloves of garlic and cubes of sugar, so their flavor carries the mitzvah into other foods — and lets many more people share in it.
Afterward — the coins
The silver is now the kohen’s. He may keep it, give it to charity, or return it to the family as a gift — customs vary. Because a kohen so often returns the coins, many families keep an engraved set as a lasting heirloom.
Choosing the silver
We don’t rule on halacha; your rabbi does that. What we can do is make sure the silver itself is right — the correct weight, honest fineness, and, if you’d like, a keepsake worth passing down. Here is what actually qualifies.
Valid for the redemption
✓
Genuine silver coins — dedicated Pidyon HaBen sets or Silver Eagles
✓
Pre-1935 US silver dollars (Morgan / Peace, 90%) — five ≈ 120 g
✓
Silverware or jewelry of sufficient value
Cannot be used
✕
Paper money or banknotes
✕
A check or credit-card payment
✕
Land, loans, IOUs, or clad / plated “silver” — at any face value
Is your family exempt — a kohen, a levi, a cesarean birth? There is nothing to buy and nothing missed. If you’d still like to mark a firstborn’s thirtieth day with a silver keepsake, we’d be glad to help; it carries no obligation of any kind.
Common Questions
Questions families ask us
What does “Pidyon HaBen” actually mean?
Literally, “redemption of the son.” It is a Torah mitzvah in which a father redeems his firstborn son from a kohen for the value of five biblical silver shekels — traditionally on the baby’s 31st day.
Who is obligated, and who is exempt?
The obligation is on the father of a firstborn son who is a peter rechem — the first to open his mother’s womb by natural birth, to two non-Kohen/non-Levi parents. There is no redemption if the father is a Kohen or Levi, if the mother is a bat-Kohen or bat-Levi, if the birth was by cesarean, if the firstborn is a girl or a daughter was born first, or (depending on the stage) after a prior pregnancy loss. Several of these need a rabbi’s ruling.
When is it held — and what if that day is Shabbat?
On the 31st day after birth (the day of birth counts as day one). If the 31st falls on Shabbat or a festival, it is deferred to the next permitted weekday, because handing over the coins is a kind of transaction. Chol HaMoed, Chanukah and Purim are not deferred.
How much silver is required?
Five sanctuary shekels, rendered as pure silver. The mainstream range is roughly 90–93 g (Sephardi) and 96–100 g (Ashkenazi), commonly summarized as “about 100 grams,” or ≈3.2 troy oz. Many dedicated sets are made to ≈117 g as a buffer so a single set clears every opinion. Follow your community’s custom.
Can I use US silver dollars, Silver Eagles, or cash?
Genuine silver works: four one-ounce Silver Eagles already exceed the weight, and five pre-1935 Morgan or Peace dollars (90% silver) hold about 120 g. Later clad or plated “silver” dollars generally do not qualify, and paper money, checks, credit, land and IOUs are never valid — they lack intrinsic value.
Why five coins — and sometimes six?
The five coins mirror the “five shekalim” the Torah names. Strictly, it is the weight that matters, not the count — but five is the beloved custom. Some families add a sixth coin as a safeguard, in case one is slightly light.
What actually happens during the ceremony?
A short scripted dialogue: the father presents his firstborn and the coins; the kohen asks whether he would rather keep the son or the five coins; the father chooses his son and hands over the silver, reciting two blessings (al pidyon haben and Sheheḥeyanu). The kohen then blesses the child. It is set within a festive meal.
What does the kohen do with the coins afterward?
They legally become his. He may keep them, give them to charity, or return them to the family as a gift once the redemption has taken effect. Many kohanim return an engraved set so the family can keep it as an heirloom.
Our situation is unusual — grown son, twins, adoption, conversion, a prior loss…
All of these have specific halachot. A grown man whose father never redeemed him redeems himself — it is never too late. With twins, only the firstborn is redeemed. Adoption, conversion timing, uncertain lineage and prior pregnancy loss each turn on details. Bring your case to a competent rabbi; the redemption can always be arranged later.
This is my first time buying silver — what should I look for?
Confirm three things: fineness (.999 or .900/.925), the total pure-silver weight in grams, and that it meets the weight for your community’s practice — ideally the ≈117 g buffer so it is valid for all. A certificate of content and clear guidance matter most. If in doubt, check the specifics with your rabbi or the officiating kohen.
Preparing for a Pidyon HaBen?
Come in to our Diamond District counter, or reach us before the thirty-first day. We’ll help you choose a set that’s right, verify its silver, and have it ready in time — whether it’s your first time buying silver or your fifth child.
